children: Scanning a range of inflation projections, it’s clear that inflation isn’t forecast to cool to the Federal Reserve’s 2% goal when the Bureau of Labor Statistics releases its September Consumer Price Index data on Wednesday.

The overall consensus estimates that September's CPI will increase 3.7% Y/Y, increasing from 3.4% in August. Excluding volatile food and energy prices, core CPI is seen rising 2.5%, from roughly 2.5% in the prior month.

In fact, Citi economist Veronica Clark doesn't expect any major shifts in the September data when compared with August. "Despite a stronger increase in August, most details of CPI were largely benign," she said in a note to clients. "We expect this dynamic to continue in September, with still-slowing shelter inflation, modest services prices overall, and limited signs of pass-through from higher energy costs to goods prices."
Truflation notes that gasoline, tariffs, and upstream costs are driving inflation risk, with housing, food, and discretionary durables providing some relief.

Even with inflation remaining stubbornly above the Fed's 2% goal, Citi doesn't expect another rate hike for the rest of the year. Traders, though, are largely pricing in another 25-basis point increase in December, putting the odds of a hike at 69.1%, rising from a 23.8% probability for the October meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool.

Truflation, a firm that tracks prices daily, sums up the potential impact on the Fed, noting that further tightening can't directly resolve energy or import supply shocks but broader pass-through into core goods and services "could justify maintaining restrictive policy."

title: CPI isn't expected to show much progress on inflation in September
